node.label: Edmund S Morgan
node.date_label: The Stamp Act Crisis (with Helen M.Morgan) (1953) · American Slavery,American Freedom (1975) · Inventing the People (1988)
node.description: Historian of early America who made the relation between slavery and freedom a central interpretive problem. In his1972 address,Morgan rejects treating enslavement as an exception to the national story or freedom as mere disguise. His Virginia-centered argument asks how racial domination and the independence claimed by white colonists developed together. Its particular mechanism remains open to debate rather than explaining every colonial society.

named_group_routes.evidence_note: The atlas’s Military history entry has no Canadian participants. Cook’s account of Stacey and the Army Historical Section (official history as archive-making and narrative) parallels the military entry’s concern with source access and narrative framing. Comparison: the Canadian field is not presented as derived from Howard or Keegan. Revision 1.142 adds an official-history strand to the Military history entry, the international parallel to Cook’s account: Edmonds’s preface (1922, read) describes a Historical Section ‘charged with the sorting and arrangement of the records’ and a history read in proof by officers who took part; Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022, pp. 65–67, read) describe British official commissions during and after the Second World War drawing academic historians to war. named_group_routes.relationship: Useful knowledge as the cause of sustained growth: the “Industrial Enlightenment”, “the key to sustained and accelerating invention” (2002 draft), which kept the early Industrial Revolution from “fizzling out” (2007 lecture); with Kelly and Ó Gráda, British workers’ human capital against Allen’s high-wage explanation (2014), and low initial wages and mechanical skills across England’s 41 counties (2023)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words, read. October 2002 draft (“The Enduring Riddle of the European Miracle”, p. 10): Enlightenment thinkers “created the attitudes, the institutions, and the mechanisms by which new knowledge was created, spread and put to good use. It is this specific aspect of the period that I have called the Industrial Enlightenment … the movement was not the key to invention; it was the key to sustained and accelerating invention.” Max Weber Lecture (EUI, 2007, pp. 2–5): countries of the 1914 “convergence club” “were countries that in the eighteenth century were subject to the European Enlightenment. This strong correlation is not in and of itself proof of causality” (p. 2); the tightening of propositional and prescriptive knowledge “prevented the early Industrial Revolution from fizzling out and enabled it to become the taproot of modern growth” (p. 5). With Morgan Kelly and Cormac Ó Gráda, “Precocious Albion” (2014, author-posted proof, pp. 16.2–16.4): “the main reason for its precocity was its higher level of human capital”; against Allen’s induced innovation, “the driver of technological progress was something deeper and stronger than cheap coal and high wages”. “The Mechanics of the Industrial Revolution” (JPE 2023, pp. 60–61): their prediction “runs directly counter to the influential argument of Allen (2009a)”; the finding concerns the 41 counties of England, not Britain’s international position. The Enlightened Economy (2009) is unread; reviewing it, Harley (EH.Net, 2010, read) wondered “if causation from Enlightenment, as an intellectual stance, to economic change actually existed” and found that it “seems almost to describe the nature of successful change at least as much as its cause.” Each quotation is tied to the text it comes from; the 2002 wording is not claimed for the 2009 book. Revision 1.145 drew this arrow from technology because Mokyr had no entry; revision 1.146 re-sources it to joel_mokyr and keeps its id. His theory of useful knowledge as such is drawn on joel_mokyr → technology.

sources.title: J. E. Edmonds, Military Operations, France and Belgium, 1914, vol. I (London: Macmillan, 1922), preface, pp. v–ix.
sources.citation: J. E. Edmonds, Military Operations, France and Belgium, 1914, vol. I (London: Macmillan, 1922), preface, pp. v–ix.

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.142 (evidence-1900-1960.md §1a): the preface, signed ‘J. E. E. April 1922’, in the University of Toronto copy (archive.org militaryoperatio01edmouoft, djvu text). Quoted: ‘THIS history has been compiled with the purpose of providing within reasonable compass an authoritative account, suitable for general readers and for students at military schools … It is based on the British official records’ (p. v); ‘written orders and messages are absolutely reliable evidence of the matters with which they deal, war diaries and reports of actions, written up immediately after events, are liable to contain mistakes’ (p. vi); the ‘Historical Section, Committee of Imperial Defence’, Military Branch, also ‘charged with the sorting and arrangement of the records dealing with operations overseas’ (pp. vi–vii); ‘The French General Staff has not yet issued any history’ (p. vii); material furnished by the director of the German Reichsarchiv (p. viii; OCR corrected); ‘The typescript or proof sheets have been read by a number of commanders and staff and regimental officers who took part in the events narrated’ (pp. viii–ix). The preface documents participant review; its effects on the history’s independence are not assessed here. Green (2003) and French (1986) remain unread.

verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.142 (evidence-1900-1960.md §§1f, 3b, 4b, 6a): pp. 55–67 read; pp. 68–76 keyword-located only (open access, CC BY-NC-ND). Quoted: the War Studies origin story is ‘seductive in its simplicity. It casts Howard as an heroic figure, almost single-handedly … delivering the study of war from the academic wilderness’, ‘a story that Howard himself consciously cultivated’ (pp. 56–57); Laughton ‘a founding member of both the Navy Records Society and The English Historical Review’ (p. 60); Howard’s 1956 article and a 1955 letter to Liddell Hart (pp. 59–60); a 1934 IHR report (p. 61); Maurice’s chair of military studies (1927) and his inaugural lecture, ‘statecraft, economics, the supply of raw material, science, and industry are factors which are of prime importance’, ‘military history is but a special branch of the general study’ (pp. 61–62); the department ‘briefly re-named War Studies in 1943, however it was closed in 1948’, and Howard used Maurice’s lecture for his 1964 inaugural (p. 63); Webster and Frankland’s official history from 1950, Webster ‘convinced … of the relevance and importance of war as a field of scholarship’ (p. 65); Hancock as head of the civil series from 1941, with Gowing, and his Country and Calling (1954), pp. 196–97, ‘the armed forces nowadays were no more than the cutting edge of the nation at war’ (pp. 66–67); Hancock among the 1946 Chichele electors choosing Falls over Liddell Hart (p. 66 n. 46, citing Strachan 2014, unread); official programmes ‘catalysed new approaches’ (p. 68, keyword-located). URL supplied at release (release/fixes-1.141.md, finding 12).
